1.baby: Pregnancy is counted from the first day of your last period, so in week 1 there is no baby yet. Conception usually happens about two weeks later. Right now your body is starting a new cycle, and in your ovaries several tiny follicles, each holding an egg, are beginning to grow.
1.body: This week you have your period, as your body sheds the lining of the womb and starts to build a fresh one. If you're hoping to conceive, it's a good moment to look after your health and habits. Tiredness, cramps or low mood around your period are common and usually ease within a few days.
tips: If you're trying to conceive, take 400 mcg of folic acid daily and continue until 12 weeks of pregnancy.
Stopping alcohol and smoking before you conceive gives your future baby the best start.
If you take regular medicines, talk to your doctor before trying rather than stopping them yourself.
todo: Note the date your last period started; it's used to estimate your due date.

2.baby: There's still no baby this week, but an egg is getting ready. Ovulation, when a mature egg is released from an ovary, usually happens about 14 days before your next period is due, so around the end of this week in a 28-day cycle. Once released, the egg can be fertilised for roughly 12 to 24 hours.
2.body: The lining of your womb is thickening, ready to welcome a fertilised egg. Around ovulation, some people notice clearer, slippery discharge or a brief twinge on one side of the lower tummy. Many notice nothing at all, which is completely normal.
tips: Trying naturally? Having sex every 2 to 3 days covers your fertile window without perfect timing.
Keep taking 400 mcg of folic acid daily; it matters most in the very first weeks.
Ovulation tests can help, but cycles vary, so go easy on yourself if timing feels stressful.

3.baby: If an egg and sperm meet in a fallopian tube, fertilisation creates a single cell carrying a full set of genetic instructions. Over the next few days it divides again and again as it travels to the womb, becoming a tiny ball of cells called a blastocyst. Towards the end of this week or early next week, it begins to attach to the lining of the womb, which is called implantation.
3.body: Most people feel no different this week, and it's still too early for a home pregnancy test to give a reliable result. Some notice mild cramps or light spotting around implantation, but many don't. If you're waiting to find out, try to fill the days with things that help you feel calm.
tips: Home tests are most reliable from the first day of a missed period, so waiting a little can save worry.
Keep taking folic acid daily; your baby's neural tube forms over the next few weeks.
Skip alcohol while you wait to find out; no amount is known to be safe in pregnancy.

4.baby: Your baby, now called an embryo, has settled into the lining of your womb and is about 2 mm long. It's protected by a fluid-filled amniotic sac, and a tiny yolk sac is providing nourishment for now. The outer layer of cells is starting to form the placenta, which will later supply oxygen and nutrients.
4.body: Your period may be due around now, and a missed period is often the first sign. Some people notice tender breasts, tiredness, mild cramps or light spotting, while others feel nothing yet. If you have bleeding, or tummy pain that worries you, especially on one side, contact a doctor or midwife.
tips: If you haven't already, start 400 mcg of folic acid daily now and continue until 12 weeks.
Keep caffeine under 200 mg a day, which is about two mugs of instant coffee.
If you take regular medicines, tell your doctor you're pregnant, and don't stop them without advice.
todo: Take a home pregnancy test if your period is late.
Contact a doctor or midwife to start your pregnancy care.

5.baby: Your baby's neural tube, which will become the brain and spinal cord, is forming quickly. A simple heart is taking shape and may start to beat around now, though it's usually too early to see on a scan. Tiny blood vessels are appearing too, and some will become the umbilical cord.
5.body: Many people find out they're pregnant around now. Rising hormones can make you feel tired or queasy, need to pee more often or notice sore breasts. It's normal to feel a mix of excitement and worry, so talk to someone you trust if it feels like a lot.
tips: Keep taking 400 mcg of folic acid daily to support your baby's developing nervous system.
Avoid alcohol and smoking; if you'd like support to stop, your doctor or midwife can help.
Rest when you can; early tiredness is real and often eases after the first trimester.
todo: List any medicines and supplements you take, to discuss at your first appointment.

6.baby: Your baby is about 6 mm long, with a curved shape and a small tail that will later disappear. Buds that will become arms and legs are appearing, and there are tiny dents where the ears will be. A flickering heartbeat can sometimes be seen on an early vaginal ultrasound.
6.body: Nausea often starts around now and can strike at any time of day, not just the morning. Eating small amounts often, resting and sipping fluids can help, and some people find ginger useful. If you can't keep food or drink down, contact your doctor or midwife, as safe treatments are available.
tips: Keep plain crackers by your bed and nibble a few before getting up if mornings feel queasy.
Try ginger tea or ginger biscuits; many people find ginger settles nausea.
Sip water through the day; small, frequent drinks are easier when you feel sick.
todo: Book your first pregnancy (booking) appointment; it usually takes place between 8 and 12 weeks.

7.baby: Your baby is now about 1 cm long from head to bottom. The brain is growing fast, so the head looks large compared with the body, and small dimples mark where the nose and ears will form. The arm buds are lengthening, and their flattened ends will soon become hands.
7.body: Your blood volume is rising to support the pregnancy, which can make you thirstier than usual. Tiredness, nausea and mood swings can make this a demanding week, and that's very common. Your womb is growing too, though most people won't look pregnant for several more weeks.
tips: Aim for about 8 glasses of fluid a day; water, milk and fruit teas all count.
Eat little and often to keep nausea in check; an empty stomach can make it worse.
When you share your news is entirely up to you.
todo: Ask which screening tests you'll be offered in the first trimester, so you have time to think about them.

8.baby: Your baby is about 1.6 cm long and growing very quickly. The arms and legs are getting longer, and fingers are beginning to form. The placenta is developing tiny branches that help it attach firmly to the wall of your womb.
8.body: You may feel bloated and notice your breasts feel fuller or tender. As your womb grows it presses on your bladder, so needing to pee more often is common. Feeling low or anxious at times is normal too, and your midwife or doctor is there to talk things through.
tips: If bathroom trips wake you at night, drink more earlier in the day and a little less in the evening.
Choose pasteurised milk and cheese, and cook meat until it's steaming hot with no pink.
Avoid liver and supplements containing vitamin A (retinol), as too much can harm your baby.
todo: Your first antenatal (booking) appointment usually happens between 8 and 12 weeks; check yours is booked.

9.baby: Your baby is now about 2.3 cm long, and the face is becoming more recognisable, with eyelids, a small mouth and a tongue with tiny taste buds. Hands and feet are developing, and all the major organs, including the heart, brain, lungs and kidneys, are growing. Bones are starting to form.
9.body: Pregnancy hormones such as hCG are around their peak, which may be why nausea and tiredness can feel strongest now. Your breasts may be bigger and your waist a little thicker. For many people, symptoms start to ease over the coming weeks.
tips: Healthy snacks like hummus with carrot sticks or a boiled egg can keep your energy steady.
Accept offers of help; it's okay to do less while your body works this hard.
Wash fruit, vegetables and salad well, and wash your hands after handling raw meat.

10.baby: Your baby is about 3 cm long and has moved from the embryo stage to the fetal stage. Fingers and toes are no longer webbed, the elbows can bend, and tiny buds for future teeth sit in the jaw. Small jerky movements can be seen on a scan, though you won't feel them for a while yet.
10.body: Bloating, wind and heartburn are common, because the hormone progesterone relaxes the muscles of your digestive system. Smaller meals, eating slowly and a short walk after eating may help. Your clothes may start to feel tighter around the waist, even before a bump shows.
tips: Try six small meals a day instead of three large ones, and avoid eating right before bed.
If it feels comfortable, gentle walking or swimming counts towards about 150 active minutes a week.
Write down questions as they come up, so they're ready for your next appointment.
todo: Ask about first-trimester screening: the combined test (usually 10 to 14 weeks) or NIPT, available from 10 weeks.

11.baby: Your baby is about 4 cm long. The head is still large for the body, but the body is catching up quickly. Fingers and toes have separated, tiny nails are starting to form, and your baby can open and close their hands, though you won't feel any movement yet.
11.body: Your body is now pumping much more blood than before, which can make you feel warm or a little dizzy at times. As your womb grows, stretching muscles and ligaments may cause mild aches low in your tummy. If pain is severe or doesn't settle, or you have any bleeding, contact your doctor or midwife.
tips: Stand up slowly, and sit down if you feel faint; keep water and a snack handy.
Ask someone else to empty the cat litter, or wear gloves and wash your hands afterwards.
Up to 2 portions of oily fish a week is good for you; avoid shark, swordfish and marlin.

12.baby: Your baby is about 5.4 cm long and weighs around 14 g. All the major organs, muscles and limbs are in place and will keep growing and maturing. Fingernails are forming, and the heartbeat can be picked up on an ultrasound scan.
12.body: Many people start to feel a little better around now as nausea and tiredness ease, though for some it takes a few more weeks. Your waist may be thickening, and you may feel hungrier. There's no need to eat for two; a varied, balanced diet is what matters.
tips: Folic acid matters most until 12 weeks; ask whether to continue a pregnancy multivitamin after that.
Ask about vitamin D; many people are advised to take a daily supplement during pregnancy.
Start pelvic floor exercises: squeeze and lift, hold for a few seconds, then relax. Repeat daily.
todo: Your dating scan (usually 10 to 14 weeks) checks your baby's development and confirms your due date.
Start thinking about where you'd like to give birth; you can always change your mind later.

13.baby: Your baby is about 7.4 cm long, and the body is starting to grow faster than the head. Vocal cords are forming, and bones are beginning to harden, starting with the skull and the long bones of the arms and legs. Your baby moves around a lot, and some babies already suck their thumbs.
13.body: You're nearing the end of the first trimester, and many people notice more energy now. As your womb rises out of your pelvis, a small bump may appear and the urge to pee often may ease. Swollen or bleeding gums are common in pregnancy, so keep brushing gently twice a day.
tips: Use a soft toothbrush, and see a dentist for a check-up; let them know you're pregnant.
If you're sick, rinse your mouth with plain water to protect your teeth.
Avoid anyone with chickenpox or rubella, and tell your midwife or doctor if you've been exposed.

14.baby: Welcome to the second trimester. Your baby is about 8.5 cm long, and the head is becoming rounder and more in proportion with the body. Your baby swallows small amounts of amniotic fluid, and the kidneys pass it back out as urine, which is good practice for later.
14.body: Many people feel more energetic in the second trimester, and your appetite may return. Your baby doesn't need extra calories yet, so healthy snacks are a good way to handle hunger between meals. You might notice yellowish marks in your bra; this is usually colostrum, the first milk.
tips: Reach for yoghurt, fruit or a handful of unsalted nuts when hunger strikes between meals.
Stay active in ways you enjoy, and stop if you feel too hot, dizzy or unwell.
If worries are weighing on you, talking to your partner, a friend or your midwife can help.
todo: Missed first-trimester screening? Ask about the second-trimester blood test, usually done around 15 to 20 weeks.

15.baby: Your baby is about 10 cm long and is growing a fine, soft layer of hair called lanugo. Eyebrows and eyelashes are starting to develop, and the eyes are sensitive to light even though the eyelids are closed. Around now, your baby may begin to hear sounds such as your heartbeat.
15.body: As your bump grows, you might feel sharp, brief twinges on the sides of your tummy, known as round ligament pain; resting usually helps. More vaginal discharge is common too. See your doctor or midwife if it changes colour, smells unpleasant, or you feel itchy or sore.
tips: Loose cotton clothing and an unperfumed moisturiser can soothe itchy, stretching skin.
Move slowly when you change position to ease round ligament twinges.
Don't hesitate to ask for a seat on public transport; your balance is changing.

16.baby: Your baby is about 11.6 cm long and weighs around 100 g. The nervous system is developing fast, so the arms and legs move more, and your baby can make fists. Facial expressions come and go too, though they're random for now while muscle control develops.
16.body: You may have an antenatal check around now, including your blood pressure and a urine test. Constipation is common, and fibre, fluids and gentle exercise can help. Some people feel the first flutters of movement between 16 and 24 weeks, often later in a first pregnancy.
tips: Fill up on fibre: wholegrains, fruit, vegetables, beans and lentils help keep things moving.
Test your home carbon monoxide alarm; it protects you and your baby.
Sex is safe in pregnancy unless your doctor or midwife has advised otherwise.
todo: Ask about the whooping cough (pertussis) vaccine — usually given between 16 and 32 weeks in the UK or 27–36 weeks in the US.

17.baby: Your baby is about 13 cm long and is starting to lay down a little fat under the skin. Fingernails are growing, and the ridges that will become unique fingerprints are forming. Your baby can move their eyes and may react to loud noises.
17.body: Your waist is gradually disappearing as your womb moves up and out, so you may look more obviously pregnant. Stretch marks may appear on your tummy, breasts or thighs; they're very common and usually fade after the birth. Hormones can make small worries feel bigger, so share how you're feeling.
tips: Moisturising won't prevent stretch marks, but it can ease dry, itchy skin.
Start comparing where you'd like to give birth: hospital, birth centre or home, where available.
Wear a supportive, comfortable bra; your breasts may have gone up a size.
todo: If you work, look into your maternity leave rights and when you need to tell your employer.

18.baby: Your baby is about 14 cm long and very active, wriggling and moving their arms and legs. Hearing is developing, along with reflexes such as swallowing and sucking. Your baby may have periods of sleep and wakefulness, and loud noises might wake them.
18.body: You might feel your baby move for the first time, often as fluttering or bubbling that's easy to mistake for wind. Your blood pressure may be a little lower than usual, so get up slowly if you feel dizzy. A dark line down your tummy, called the linea nigra, is normal and usually fades after the birth.
tips: Get out of bed by rolling onto your side first, then pushing up with your arms.
If you'd rather not know your baby's sex at the scan, tell the sonographer before it starts.
Sleep with a pillow between your knees if your hips or back ache at night.
todo: Your detailed anomaly (anatomy) scan is usually done between about 18 and 22 weeks; check it's booked.

19.baby: Your baby is about 15 cm long and steadily putting on weight. A protective, waxy coating called vernix is starting to cover the skin. Behind the first set of tooth buds, the buds for adult teeth are beginning to form.
19.body: The hormone relaxin is loosening your ligaments, so some activities, such as running, may start to feel uncomfortable. Sleep can be harder to come by, and aches in your back, hips or pelvis are common. If pelvic pain makes walking or turning over in bed difficult, mention it, as physiotherapy can help.
tips: Swap high-impact exercise for swimming, walking or pregnancy yoga if your joints feel loose.
Use pillows to support your bump and back; lying on your side with knees bent is often most comfortable.
Wear flat, supportive shoes to help your balance and ease back strain.

20.baby: You're halfway there. From now on, babies are usually measured from head to heel, and yours is about 25.6 cm long and weighs around 300 g. Your baby is covered in a creamy layer called vernix and may suck their thumb, which helps develop the sucking reflex.
20.body: Your bump is growing steadily, and you may wake at night with sudden calf cramps; pulling your toes up towards you can ease them. Many people notice their baby's movements more clearly from around now. If your anomaly scan hasn't happened yet, it's likely to be around this time.
tips: Stretch your calves gently before bed and stay active during the day to help prevent cramps.
Iron-rich foods like red meat, beans, lentils and leafy greens help keep your energy up.
Talk or sing to your bump if you like; your baby is starting to hear sounds from outside.
todo: If you work, ask your doctor or midwife for any pregnancy certificate you need for maternity leave or pay.
Not had the whooping cough vaccine yet? In the UK it's often offered around now, so ask about it.

21.baby: Your baby is about 26.7 cm long and now weighs more than the placenta. Movements are becoming stronger and more coordinated, and your baby is settling into patterns of sleeping and waking. Your baby can now hear noises and voices from outside the womb.
21.body: Your centre of gravity is shifting and your joints are looser, so you may feel a little unsteady. If you have a fall, try not to panic, as your baby is well protected, but do let your midwife or doctor know. You may also notice your baby is busiest just as you settle down to rest.
tips: Aim for at least 5 portions of fruit and vegetables a day, choosing wholegrains where you can.
Nap when you can to make up for disturbed nights.
Hold handrails on stairs and take extra care on wet or icy ground.

22.baby: Your baby is about 27.8 cm long. The lungs are developing, and your baby practises breathing movements and swallows small amounts of amniotic fluid. Taste buds are developing too, and your baby's grip is getting stronger.
22.body: Stretch marks, an achy back and occasional tightening across your bump are all common now. Aches and pains are normal in pregnancy, but if you're unsure whether something is serious, check with your midwife or doctor. Call straight away if you have severe pain or any bleeding from the vagina.
tips: Sit with your back supported, and take breaks from standing to ease backache.
Make a simple wellbeing plan: what helps you feel calm, and who you can call on tough days.
If you smoke, it's never too late to stop, and support services can make it much easier.
todo: Look into antenatal (birth preparation) classes; many book up a few weeks ahead.

23.baby: Your baby is about 28.9 cm long, and the limbs are now in proportion with the body. They're practising breathing, settling into sleeping and waking patterns, and starting to gain fat more quickly. Over the coming weeks you may see your tummy move when your baby kicks.
23.body: You may feel more breathless as your growing womb presses upwards, and your ribs may ache as your rib cage expands. Your breasts might leak a little colostrum. Start getting to know your baby's usual pattern of movements, and contact your midwife or maternity unit if it slows down or changes.
tips: Swap some cups of tea or coffee for water or fruit tea to stay under 200 mg of caffeine a day.
Your skin burns more easily in pregnancy, so use a high-factor sunscreen and seek shade at midday.
Put your feet up and rest when you feel breathless.

24.baby: Your baby is about 30 cm long and weighs around 600 g. The lungs are formed but not yet ready to work on their own, and the skin is still thin and a little wrinkled while fat builds up underneath. Babies born from around now can be cared for in a neonatal unit, though every extra week in the womb makes a real difference.
24.body: Aches around your ribs, back or bump are common as your ligaments loosen and your baby grows. From now on, get urgent advice if you have a severe headache, blurred vision or flashing lights, pain just below your ribs, or sudden swelling of your face, hands or feet. These can be signs of pre-eclampsia, which needs checking quickly.
tips: Don't use a home doppler to check on your baby; if you're worried about movements, call your maternity unit.
Save your maternity unit's phone number in your phone and keep a copy in your bag.
It's a nice time to start thinking about what matters to you for the birth.
todo: A glucose test for gestational diabetes is often done between 24 and 28 weeks; ask if it's recommended for you.

25.baby: Your baby is about 34.6 cm long and filling out as more fat is laid down, so the skin looks smoother. A loud noise might make your baby jump, and you may feel the occasional rhythmic jerk of hiccups. Your baby passes urine into the amniotic fluid, which helps keep it at the right level.
25.body: Mild swelling of your feet and ankles is common, especially in warm weather or at the end of the day. Mention any swelling to your midwife or doctor, and seek urgent advice if it comes on suddenly or affects your face or hands. Heartburn may also flare as your baby takes up more room.
tips: Put your feet up when you can, and avoid standing still for long periods.
For heartburn, eat smaller meals, sit upright while eating and avoid lying down soon afterwards.
If your partner plans to take leave around the birth, now is a good time for them to check their rights.
todo: If you work, check you've told your employer in time for maternity leave and pay; deadlines vary by country.

26.baby: Your baby is about 35.6 cm long, and around now the eyes open for the first time. The lungs are starting to make surfactant, a substance that will help them breathe after birth. Your baby is also making melanin, which gives colour to the skin and eyes.
26.body: As you approach the third trimester, you may feel more tired, clumsy or forgetful, which is understandable with so much going on. Leg cramps may wake you at night. If you ever feel your baby's movements slow down or stop, contact your midwife or maternity unit straight away rather than waiting.
tips: Give yourself extra time for everyday things; your body is doing a lot.
Circle your feet and flex your ankles a few times a day to ease cramps and swelling.
Lists and phone reminders can help with forgetfulness.

27.baby: Your baby is about 36.6 cm long and getting plumper every day as fat fills out the skin. The lungs and nervous system keep maturing, and your baby can open their eyes and blink. This is the last week of the second trimester.
27.body: Bloating and constipation are common now, as your growing baby squeezes your stomach and progesterone slows digestion. Snoring may start too, because the lining of your nose can swell in pregnancy. Nap when you can if tiredness is catching up with you.
tips: From 28 weeks, go to sleep on your side; if you wake up on your back, simply turn over.
Planning to fly? Check your airline's rules, as many ask for a letter from your doctor or midwife later on.
Choose wholegrain bread and pasta and drink plenty of water to help with constipation.
todo: If your blood group is Rh (D) negative, ask about anti-D; it's often offered around 28 weeks.

28.baby: Welcome to the third trimester. Your baby is about 37.6 cm long and weighs around 1 kg. Their heart beats at about 140 beats a minute, still much faster than yours, and the eyelids can open and close.
28.body: Over the coming weeks you may feel more tired and uncomfortable, with heartburn, backache or nosebleeds. Swelling in your ankles, feet or face is often due to water retention, but get it checked in case it's pre-eclampsia. Rest helps with many symptoms, and your midwife or doctor is there if anything worries you.
tips: Go to sleep on your side, including for naps; research shows it's safer for your baby.
Wash your hands often, especially after contact with young children, to lower your risk of infections.
For a nosebleed, sit up, lean forward and pinch just above your nostrils for 10 to 15 minutes.
todo: Ask about the RSV vaccine: offered from 28 weeks in the UK, or at 32 to 36 weeks during RSV season in the US.
If you're Rh (D) negative, you may be offered anti-D around now.

29.baby: Your baby is about 38.6 cm long and fully formed; the coming weeks are about maturing organs and gaining weight. The soft, downy hair called lanugo is starting to disappear. Kicks may feel more like pokes and jabs as space gets tighter.
29.body: You may feel breathless as your baby pushes up against your lungs, and you might need the toilet more at night. Your baby has their own sleep and wake pattern, often busiest when you lie down. Get to know that pattern, and contact your midwife or maternity unit straight away if it changes or slows down.
tips: Support your bump with a pillow and place another between your knees for more comfortable sleep.
Start a birth plan: think about pain relief options and who you'd like as your birth partner.
Calcium-rich foods like dairy or fortified alternatives support your baby's growing bones.

30.baby: Your baby is about 39.9 cm long, and their eyes can now focus, though vision will keep developing after birth. The brain is growing quickly, and your baby is getting better at controlling their own body temperature. Fat continues to build up under the skin.
30.body: Climbing stairs may leave you out of breath, and sleep can be patchy. Vivid or unsettling dreams are common, fuelled by hormones and the big changes ahead, and talking them through can help. If stress or low mood is building, let your midwife or doctor know.
tips: Read up on the stages of labour so you know what to expect; every birth is different.
Gather a few newborn basics; babies outgrow first-size clothes quickly, so you don't need many.
A short evening walk or gentle stretches can help you sleep better.
todo: Plan where your baby will sleep: a cot or Moses basket with a firm, flat, well-fitting mattress is safest.

31.baby: Your baby is about 41.1 cm long and very active, with somersaults, stretches and finger-sucking. Day by day they look plumper and less wrinkled. Your baby is starting to recognise voices from outside the womb, so loved ones can talk to the bump too.
31.body: You may notice your bump tightening for 20 to 30 seconds and then relaxing. These are Braxton Hicks, or practice contractions, and they shouldn't hurt. If tightenings become painful or regular before 37 weeks, contact your midwife or maternity unit, as it could be early labour.
tips: Think about how you'd like to feed your baby; your midwife can talk you through breast, bottle or both.
If Braxton Hicks feel uncomfortable, try changing position or having a warm bath.
Keep up gentle exercise if it feels good; swimming takes the weight off your joints.

32.baby: Your baby is about 42.4 cm long, fully formed, and now mainly putting on weight. Much of the fat gained over the next few weeks will help your baby stay warm after birth. Many babies have turned head down by now, but there's still time if yours hasn't.
32.body: Walking may feel more like a waddle as your body adjusts to the extra weight. Your baby has less room, but you should keep feeling movements in the same pattern right up until labour. If movements slow down, change or stop, contact your midwife or maternity unit immediately, day or night.
tips: Avoid heavy lifting, and ask for extra breaks and a seat at work if you need them.
Read about vitamin K for newborns, so you can decide in advance how you'd like it given.
Rest with your feet up for a while each day.
todo: Write your birth plan and share it with your midwife or doctor; you can change it at any time.
If you haven't had the whooping cough vaccine yet, ask about it now.

33.baby: Your baby is about 43.7 cm long, and the brain and nervous system are well developed. The bones are hardening, except for the skull, which stays soft and flexible to help your baby through birth. Your baby's pupils can now change size in response to light.
33.body: Feeling heavy and tired is very understandable now. Braxton Hicks may become more frequent as your womb gets ready for birth. A heavy feeling low in your pelvis can be a sign your baby is settling head down.
tips: Save your maternity unit's number, your birth partner's number and the hospital address in your phone.
Plan how you'll get to the hospital; it isn't safe to drive yourself while in labour.
Short, frequent rests are fine; you don't need to push through tiredness.
todo: Start packing your hospital bag, so you're ready if your baby comes early.
Choose a car seat for the journey home, ideally a new one, and practise fitting it.

34.baby: Your baby is about 45 cm long and curled up with legs bent towards the chest, as space is getting tight. The fingernails have reached the fingertips. You should still feel your baby shifting about and see your bump change shape.
34.body: If your baby moves down into your pelvis, breathing and heartburn may ease, though you may need to pee more often. This doesn't mean birth is about to happen; it may still be weeks away. Leaking a little colostrum is normal, and a supportive bra can help with tender breasts.
tips: Keep moving gently each day, even if it's just a short walk.
If you work, plan your maternity leave start date; many people stop around now.
Stock up on maternity pads for after the birth.
todo: Talk to your midwife or doctor about pain relief options for labour, and note your preferences in your birth plan.

35.baby: Your baby is about 46.2 cm long and getting chubbier, which will help them stay warm after birth. The brain is still growing fast. It's cramped in there now, but you should feel movements as strongly and regularly as before.
35.body: Sore ribs are common as your baby kicks from a head-down position. Severe pain under the ribs, though, can be a sign of pre-eclampsia, so call your midwife or doctor if you notice it. Many people start maternity leave around now; do what feels right for you.
tips: Practise slow breathing now, in through your nose and out through your mouth; it can help in labour.
Consider a well-fitting nursing bra and some breast pads.
Batch-cook a few meals for the freezer while you have the energy.
todo: Pack your hospital bag: notes, comfy clothes, nightwear, maternity pads, snacks, baby clothes and nappies.

36.baby: Your baby is about 47.4 cm long, and the lungs are probably mature enough to breathe without help. The soft lanugo hair is mostly gone, and your baby may have hair on their head. Many babies have now settled head down, ready for birth.
36.body: Your check-up around now will look at your blood pressure, urine and the size of your bump, so try to keep these appointments even when getting there feels like an effort. If your baby isn't head down, you may be offered a procedure to help them turn. A little leaking of urine when you laugh or cough is common, and pelvic floor exercises help.
tips: Keep your notes, birth plan and important numbers somewhere easy to grab.
Do your pelvic floor exercises daily; they help now and with recovery after the birth.
Take a few quiet minutes each day to relax your body and mind.
todo: Check your hospital bag is packed and the car seat is ready for the journey home.
Ask about group B strep (GBS); in the US, testing is usually done between 36 and 38 weeks.

37.baby: Your baby is about 48.6 cm long and, if born now, would no longer be considered premature. Around 95% of babies are head down by this point. Your baby is trying out facial expressions such as frowning and smiling, and the toenails have reached the tips of the toes.
37.body: You may notice more discharge and more Braxton Hicks, along with a sudden urge to clean and organise, known as nesting. Signs that labour may be starting include regular contractions, a show (a plug of sticky mucus), backache or your waters breaking. Call your midwife or maternity unit if your waters break, you have any bleeding, or your baby's movements change.
tips: Nesting is natural, but pace yourself and rest as much as you can.
Learn the signs of labour and when your maternity unit would like you to call.
Read about the baby blues and postnatal depression, and share what you learn with your partner or a close friend.
todo: Plan who will look after any other children or pets when labour starts.

38.baby: Your baby is about 49.8 cm long and weighs around 3 kg. Most of the lanugo has gone, and the bowels are storing meconium, which will be your baby's first poo. Reflexes such as grasping and sucking are ready for life outside.
38.body: Waiting can bring a mix of impatience, excitement and nerves, and all of that is normal. At your appointment around now, your blood pressure, urine and bump will be checked, and you may talk about what happens if you go past your due date. A short walk and some fresh air can help the time pass.
tips: Take your maternity notes with you whenever you go out.
Keep easy snacks and drinks ready for early labour, like bananas or yoghurt.
Put a waterproof sheet on your mattress if you're worried about your waters breaking at night.
todo: Ask what your care team offers if you go past your due date, such as a membrane sweep or induction.

39.baby: Your baby is about 50.7 cm long and is now full term. The skin has developed a thicker outer layer that helps protect the body and control temperature. Some vernix may remain on the skin at birth, or most of it may be gone.
39.body: More discharge, pressure low in your bump and backache are common as your baby moves down. Call your midwife or maternity unit if your waters break, you have any bleeding, or your baby's movements change. Call urgently, too, for a severe headache, vision problems, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling, severe itching or a fever.
tips: Contractions lasting about 60 seconds, every 5 minutes, are a common cue to call; follow your unit's advice.
If your waters break, note the time and the colour of the fluid, then call your maternity unit.
Rest when you can; early labour can take a while, and sleep helps you save energy.
todo: Confirm how you'll get to the hospital and who will come with you.

40.baby: Your baby is about 51.2 cm long and weighs around 3.4 kg, though healthy babies come in a wide range of sizes. It's snug in there, but your baby should still be moving in their usual pattern. Only about 1 in 20 babies arrive on their due date, so any day around now is right on time.
40.body: If this is your first baby, you'll usually have a check this week with blood pressure, urine and bump measurements. Real contractions tend to become stronger, longer and closer together, while Braxton Hicks stay irregular. Your baby's movements shouldn't slow down or stop; if they do, contact your maternity unit straight away, at any hour.
tips: If contractions start at night, try to rest or sleep through the early ones.
During the day, staying upright and moving around can help labour progress.
There's no proven way to safely bring on labour at home, so check with your midwife before trying anything.
todo: Discuss a membrane sweep with your midwife or doctor; it's often offered around 40 to 41 weeks.

41.baby: Your baby is simply taking a little extra time, which is common, especially in a first pregnancy. Most babies weigh around 3 to 4 kg by now, and the fastest growth is behind them. Babies born after their due date often have dry, peeling skin, which settles on its own within a few days.
41.body: Going past your due date can feel frustrating, so be gentle with yourself. From 41 weeks the risks, while still small, start to rise, so your midwife or doctor will talk with you about extra monitoring, a membrane sweep or induction. Keep paying attention to your baby's movements, and call straight away if they change.
tips: Ask as many questions as you need about induction; it's a decision you make together with your care team.
Keep your phone charged and your bag by the door.
Gentle walks, warm baths and plenty of rest can help you stay comfortable while you wait.
todo: Talk through your options with your midwife or doctor: extra monitoring, a membrane sweep or a date for induction.

42.baby: Your baby is fully developed and simply taking their time. Babies born after 42 weeks may have long nails, dry or peeling skin and little vernix left; the skin usually settles within a few days. Your care team will keep a close eye on you both.
42.body: A pregnancy that continues beyond 42 weeks is called post-term, and induction is usually recommended by this point. If you've chosen to wait, you'll usually be offered closer monitoring, such as checks of your baby's heart rate and the fluid around them. Contact your maternity unit straight away if your baby's movements change, your waters break, or you have any bleeding.
tips: It's okay to feel impatient or fed up; lean on the people who support you.
Ask your care team to explain each option, with its benefits and risks, so you can decide together.
Keep eating regularly and drinking water so you have energy for labour.
todo: If you haven't already, agree a plan with your care team for induction or closer monitoring.
